source.title_on_document: The Application of Multimodal Generative AI in College English Creative Writing Instruction

supplement.holds: No separate supplement or online appendix is identified. Figures are included at the end of this PDF (pp. 17-21); they are not a separate supplement. No location for missing SDs, SEs, group-specific analyses, or analyzed participant counts is given.

paper_design_summary: The paper describes an eight-week college creative-writing intervention involving 60 first-year non-English-major students, with 30 assigned to multimodal AI instruction and 30 to traditional instruction; it simultaneously calls the design quasi-experimental and says students were randomly assigned (p. 7, sections 3.2-3.3). Teachers evaluated writing, and the results present pretest/posttest language and creativity scores without identifying group-specific results or analyzed participant counts (pp. 8, 11-12). A nested comparison contrasts student-generated and AI-generated images using 30 works, which is an output-source comparison rather than an additional participant experiment (p. 13, Table 5).

studies.label: College English creative-writing instruction, with nested human-versus-AI image comparison

assignment.what_was_assigned: Students are explicitly said to be randomly assigned to experimental AI instruction or traditional instruction. The field_rct label provisionally follows this literal statement and the course setting; the same paragraph calls the design quasi-experimental and describes two natural classes. No randomization procedure or reconciliation of class membership with individual assignment is provided (p. 7, section 3.2).
assignment.quote: Using a quasi-experimental design, students are randomly assigned to an experimental group and a control group (30 each).
assignment.locator: p. 7, section 3.2; pp. 7-8, section 3.3 (between-group instruction with repeated pretest/posttest assessment)

arms.name: Multimodal generative AI instruction
arms.description: Experimental instruction using ChatGPT, Midjourney and DALL·E for ideas, drafting, revision and visual expression with teacher guidance; assignment count is 30 (p. 7, section 3.2).

arms.name: Traditional instruction
arms.description: Conventional writing instruction, group brainstorming, independent drafting and teacher feedback/correction, without the experimental AI tools; assignment count is 30 (pp. 7-8, sections 3.2-3.3). This is ordinary teaching rather than a separate experimentally added aid.

participants.exclusions: No exclusions, attrition, realized analyzed total, or per-outcome participant counts are reported. The total of 60 and the 30-per-arm figures are reported in the sampling/assignment description, not in an analysis flow. The statement that all students submit final works describes the procedure (p. 8); Table 5 reports 30 works, not 30 analyzed people (p. 13).
participants.who: First-year non-English-major university students in two natural classes at one university (p. 7, section 3.2; p. 15, section 6.3). Two teachers and one AI technical staff member support the study; they are not additional students producing the scored writing (p. 7, section 3.2).
participants.quote: The study targets 60 first-year non-English major university students (divided into two natural classes).
participants.locator: p. 7, section 3.2 (60 students and 30 per group); p. 8, sections 3.3-3.4; pp. 11-13, Tables 2, 4 and 5; p. 15, section 6.3

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT, Midjourney, DALL·E; model versions not stated (p. 7, section 3.2).
ai_tool.how_used: Teacher-guided student prompting for ideas, metaphors, outlines and draft text; iterative student revision and AI feedback; persona prompts; image generation from keywords or paragraphs, and multimodal presentation. The role also includes refinement and image generation (pp. 7-10, sections 3.2-3.3 and 4.2).

task.description: English poems, stories and prose on cultural narratives, ecological writing and identity themes; students create and revise texts and add images/multimodal presentations (pp. 7-10, sections 3.3 and 4.1-4.3). Table 5 additionally compares student-generated and AI-generated visual interpretations (p. 13).
task.duration: Eight weeks, 16 sessions, two per week; initiation in Weeks 1-2, practice in Weeks 3-6, presentation in Week 7 and evaluation in Week 8 (pp. 7-8, section 3.3). No per-writing-task time limit stated.

outcomes.name: Composite creativity score
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Torrance-framework scoring of AI-assisted texts: the paper explicitly says AI-assisted texts were scored (p. 12, section 5.2.1). General writing evaluation uses two teachers, cross-validated with Grammarly and ChatGPT scoring modules (p. 8, section 3.4); teacher and AI scores are not reported separately. Table 4 gives pretest/posttest means without identifying the group, analyzed people, scored text count, scale range, or score aggregation. Unit is output because the text says texts were scored; a participant-level analysis is not established. The relationship to the separately scheduled creativity post-test is unclear (p. 8, section 3.3.4). No removal of AI is stated, so this is not coded after_ai. Composite is listed first by the codebook preference; the paper does not designate a primary outcome. The conclusion reports a different creativity scale/result without explaining its relation to Table 4.

eligibility.reason: The explicit student-randomization claim supports a provisional field_rct code, but the same paragraph labels the study quasi-experimental and refers to two natural classes without explaining the allocation procedure (p. 7, section 3.2). Sixty students and 30 per group are given at sampling/assignment, but no analyzed participant total establishes the at-least-50-analyzed-people criterion (pp. 7-8, 11-13). Criterion 3 is met because AI-assisted texts were scored for creativity using the Torrance framework, with numerical output scores in Table 4 (p. 12, section 5.2.1); general teacher scoring is described on p. 8, section 3.4. Numerical results are primarily pretest/posttest, without separate control-group results or uncertainty. The Table 5 image subanalysis is AI-versus-human output context and does not establish an effect of assistance on human output (p. 13). No independent observational study is established, so context_class is none for the main intervention pending clarification.

one_line_finding: The paper reports a composite creativity pretest mean of 5.5 and posttest mean of 7.0 (printed improvement +27.3%), but supplies no group-specific comparison, analyzed participant count or uncertainty (p. 12, Table 4).
open_questions: Were individuals actually randomized, or were the two natural classes used as intact groups, and why is the design also called quasi-experimental (p. 7, section 3.2)?
How many people were analyzed in each instructional arm and each outcome, and were there exclusions or missing assessments (pp. 7-8, 11-13)?

Whose pretest/posttest means appear in Tables 2 and 4: the AI arm, both arms pooled, or another subset? Are the control-group results and the planned SDs, t-tests and ANOVA results available (p. 8, section 3.5; pp. 11-12, Tables 2 and 4)?
Was AI available during the Week 8 writing/creativity post-tests, and are the AI-assisted texts scored in section 5.2.1 the same outputs as those post-tests (p. 8, section 3.3.4; p. 12)?

How do the conclusion's creativity means of 3.4 and 4.6 out of 5 and writing increase of 12.6% relate to the 5.5/7.0 creativity means in Table 4 and +22.2% writing increase in Table 2 (pp. 11-12, 14)?
Which construct is intended by each identically labelled Syntactic Complexity row in Table 2 (p. 11)?
How do the 30 works in Table 5 map to students and image sources, were images paired, and what rubric and raters produced the image scores (p. 13, section 5.2.2)?
notes: Screened on 2026-10-09. The entire markdown conversion was read in order, including the references and end figures; there is no appendix identified in the document. Design, counts and each cited numerical result were checked against PDF text; Tables 2, 4 and 5 and Figures 1, 2 and 5 were also visually inspected from in-memory PDF renders. No external versions or other screening forms were consulted. One classroom experiment is recorded: the nested image-source comparison is distinguished by comparison_type ai_vs_human and question none rather than inflated into an independent participant study. The declared two instructional arms have no extractable numerical between-arm contrast; phase labels in before_after contrasts are not additional randomized arms. Field_rct, randomized=yes and individual record the literal random-assignment claim, while eligibility remains unclear because of the contradictory description and absent analyzed counts. Country is not explicitly reported for the sample; the university affiliation and Chinese policy context are not treated as an explicit study-location statement. Fifteen main output outcomes are listed, with the creativity composite first; no outcome is explicitly designated primary. To respect the outcome cap, the voice and spelling error-rate branches of Figure 1 (p. 17) are omitted. The descriptive image element-completeness, abstraction and conceptual-transformation percentages in section 5.2.2 (p. 13) are also not expanded into separate outcomes because the corpus, denominators and matched constructs are not defined. The detailed image-component percentages are descriptive breakdowns, not additional human-assistance contrasts. Self-reported motivation, satisfaction, perceived creativity and concerns are excluded from output outcomes. The arm_means_sds_ns availability category is used for the printed mean summaries only: no SDs or analyzed participant Ns accompany them; N = 30 in Table 5 counts works only. This flag must not be interpreted as a complete means/SDs/N extraction. No effect sizes or corrected percentages were computed. The reported fluency percentage is transcribed as printed. Figure 2 visually plots creativity scores despite being captioned as an AI collaboration frequency line chart; it is not a distinct outcome. Figure 5 is a pie chart with a different presentation from Table 5, so image numerical contrasts are transcribed from Table 5 and its supporting prose, not reconstructed from pie shares. No evidence on diversity across people is reported. No claim of significant improvement is treated as a supplied p-value. Immediate timing denotes the within-intervention/end-of-course assessment; no delayed follow-up is reported (pp. 7-8; p. 15, section 6.3). Formal post-test AI access and the image-specific scoring method remain unresolved as described in the outcome details.
